title: Forecast Collapse in Time-Series Foundation Models
hook: Ask a forecasting model to predict hourly stock returns and it hedges into a nearly flat line — technically well-calibrated, useless for ranking. Per-series metrics never show you this.
key_points: Forecasting hourly returns for 1,000 US equities, predictions go nearly flat and rank stocks poorly — the authors call this forecast collapse.
It largely vanishes when forecasting trading volume in the same setup, so it tracks how predictable the target is, not the model.
Two causes: low predictability caps the amplitude of a calibrated point forecast, and per-series objectives never learn cross-series structure.
The result is a calibration-ranking tradeoff: minimizing squared error flattens forecasts; optimizing cross-sectional correlation can inflate amplitude by over an order of magnitude.
CalibRank, their proposed objective, balances the two — nearly tripling cross-sectional correlation on Finance1K while keeping amplitude near target.
The broader lesson: per-series metrics can hide failures in exactly the cross-series structure downstream decisions depend on.
content_html: The setup sounds routine: point a time-series foundation model at hourly returns for a thousand US stocks. The output is nearly a flat line. It scores fine on the usual metrics, and it is worthless for deciding which stock to buy.
extra_html:
Shu Wan and colleagues name this forecast collapse and trace it across time-series foundation models, twelve deep-learning forecasters, and 97 public benchmark configurations. It is tied to target predictability rather than to any one architecture — swap returns for trading volume in the same setup and it largely disappears. Two mechanisms drive it: when a target is barely predictable, a calibrated point forecast can only take a small amplitude; and per-series training objectives leave the cross-series structure unidentified entirely.

That produces a calibration-ranking tradeoff. Optimizing squared error gives you flat predictions; optimizing cross-sectional correlation directly improves ranking but can inflate forecast amplitude by more than an order of magnitude. Their proposed objective, CalibRank, balances the two: on the Finance1K benchmark it nearly triples cross-sectional correlation while keeping amplitude close to target, and improves correlation on every model tested. The transferable takeaway is about evaluation, not finance — a per-series metric can be green across the board while the cross-series structure your decisions rest on is missing. arXiv, August 2026.

related.title: Beyond IID: How General Are Tabular Foundation Models, Really?
related.hook: Tabular foundation models look great on standard IID benchmarks — but on temporal, grouped, high-dimensional, and non-IID data, plain tree-based models still win.

related.title: When Your Top Feature Makes Predictions Worse
related.hook: A feature can top your model's importance ranking and still hurt accuracy. The only way to be sure it helps: delete it, retrain, and compare on held-out data.

flashcards.back_html: When a forecasting model's predictions become nearly flat and rank series poorly — observed here on hourly returns for 1,000 US equities, measured by cross-sectional correlation.

flashcards.prompt: Why does minimizing squared error tend to flatten forecasts on low-predictability targets?

choices.text: Low predictability caps the amplitude a well-calibrated point forecast can take
Squared error is undefined for financial returns
The model runs out of capacity and underfits every series

flashcards.explanation_html: A calibrated point forecast hedges toward the mean when the target is barely predictable, so the safe answer is a small, flat one — accurate on average, useless for ranking.

flashcards.prompt: What blind spot in conventional time-series evaluation does this expose?
flashcards.back_html: Per-series metrics can look fine while the model has learned no cross-series structure — the ranking information downstream decisions actually need. Forecast volume and the collapse mostly disappears; forecast returns and it does not.
